>[!note] Binary Options
>A **binary option**, or digital option, pays a fixed amount or nothing, depending on a trigger. It is one of the simplest [[2.3.6 Exotic Options|exotic options]]. An exotic option is a contract whose payoff rule differs from a standard call or put. Binaries are priced here in the Black-Scholes-Merton setting. The stock price $S$ follows geometric Brownian motion with volatility $\sigma$. The risk-free rate $r$ and the dividend yield $q$ are constant and continuously compounded.
>
>Let $\tau = T - t$ be the time to expiry, $H$ the cash amount, and $K$ the trigger. Let $I_K = 1$ if $S_T \ge K$ and $0$ otherwise, and let $N$ be the standard normal CDF. The [[2.3.3f Black-Scholes-Merton Formula|BSM formula]] defines
>$$d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r - q + \sigma^2/2)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{\tau}.$$
>Here $N(d_2)$ is the risk-neutral probability that $S_T \ge K$. The four European binaries pay at $T$.
>- A **cash call** pays $HI_K$ and is worth $He^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$.
>- An **asset call** pays $S_TI_K$ and is worth $Se^{-q\tau}N(d_1)$.
>- A **cash put** pays $H(1 - I_K)$ and is worth $He^{-r\tau}N(-d_2)$.
>- An **asset put** pays $S_T(1 - I_K)$ and is worth $Se^{-q\tau}N(-d_1)$.
>
>The identity $\max(S_T - K, 0) = S_TI_K - KI_K$ makes a European call an asset call minus $K$ unit cash calls. A European put is $K$ unit cash puts minus an asset put. Write $b(K)$ for the value of a unit cash call. It is the limit of a narrow call spread on the call prices $c(K)$:
>$$b(K) = -\lim_{\eta \to 0}\frac{c(K + \eta) - c(K)}{\eta} = -\frac{\partial c}{\partial K}.$$
>Here $\eta$ is the gap between the two strikes. Dealers quote $b(K)$ as a [[2.3.2a Vertical Spread|call spread]] with a finite $\eta$. Two American binaries depend on the whole path up to $T$.
>- A **one-touch** pays $H$ if $S$ reaches the trigger $K$ at any time before $T$.
>- A **no-touch** pays $H$ if $S$ never reaches $K$ before $T$.
>
>Exactly one of the two pays, so their risk-neutral probabilities sum to one. When both pay at $T$, the pair is a bond worth $He^{-r\tau}$. Under constant parameters both have closed forms. Binaries are sold alone and also appear inside other products. Examples are range options, range accruals, [[2.3.6.3d Principal-Protected Notes|principal-protected notes]] and [[2.3.6.3b Autocallables|autocallables]].

>[!warning] Notation
>The lecture writes the unit cash call as $b_c(K)$. This note writes $b(K)$, and it writes vega as $\mathcal{V}$, as in [[2.3.4c Vega and Rho]].

# Intuition

A binary option is a bet on where the price ends. Its payoff jumps from $0$ to $H$ at the trigger. Before expiry the jump is smoothed out. A cash call pays $H$ with risk-neutral probability $N(d_2)$, discounted at $r$. Far from expiry this probability changes slowly with $S$. Close to expiry the price has little time to move. The probability is then near $0$ below $K$ and near $1$ above it. The value steepens into the step of the payoff. A dealer who hedges a binary must trade large amounts of stock near $K$ in its last days.

The surface shows a unit cash call with $K = 100$, $r = 4\%$, $q = 1\%$, $\sigma = 25\%$ and expiry $T = 1$. The stock price $S$ runs to the right, and calendar time $t$ runs into the page from $0$ to $0.99$. At $t = 0$ the value is a smooth S-shaped curve, worth $0.48$ at the strike. Toward the back the curve steepens into the step at $K$. The red line at $S = K$ stays near $0.5$. A price at the strike is about equally likely to end above or below it. The blue line at $S = 90$ falls from $0.32$ to almost zero. Each slice at a fixed $t$ is a discounted risk-neutral probability. It solves the BSM equation with the step as its final condition ([[7.8 Feynman-Kac Formula]]).

# Properties

#### *(Replication by Call Spreads)* A cash binary is the limit of a call spread, and dealers quote it as a spread of finite width.

Buy $1/\eta$ calls at $K - \eta$ and sell $1/\eta$ calls at $K$. The position pays $0$ below $K - \eta$ and $1$ above $K$, and it rises in a straight line between the strikes. So it pays at least as much as the unit binary in every state. The same spread with strikes $K$ and $K + \eta$ pays at most as much. A portfolio that pays more in every state costs more, which brackets the binary's price:
$$\frac{c(K) - c(K + \eta)}{\eta} \le b(K) \le \frac{c(K - \eta) - c(K)}{\eta}.$$
Both bounds tend to $-\partial c/\partial K$ as $\eta \to 0$. The centered spread $[c(K - \eta) - c(K + \eta)]/(2\eta)$ has the same limit. A dealer who sells a binary can hedge it statically by buying the first spread, which never pays less. A dealer who buys a binary hedges by selling the second spread. The width depends on the side of the market, the shape of the volatility skew, and the competition among dealers. The skew enters through the call prices, since each strike trades at its own implied volatility. A narrower spread gives a tighter quote but needs $1/\eta$ calls in each leg. Differentiating $b(K) = -\partial c/\partial K$ in $S$ gives the hedge ratio $\Delta_b(K) = -\partial\Delta_c(K)/\partial K$. Here $\Delta_c(K)$ is the delta of the call with strike $K$.

#### *(Uses)* Range options, range accruals, principal-protected notes and autocallable coupons are built from binaries.

A **digital spread** is long one binary and short another with a higher trigger. Several products are built from binaries in this way.
- A **range option** pays $H$ if $K_1 \le S_T < K_2$. It is long $H$ unit cash calls at $K_1$ and short $H$ at $K_2$, so it is worth $H[b(K_1) - b(K_2)]$.
- A **range accrual** pays $H$ for each period $(t_{i-1}, t_i)$ in which the price stays inside $(K_1, K_2)$. A floor sets a minimum total. Its payoff at $T = t_n$ is $\max\big(\text{floor},\, H\sum_{i=1}^{n} I_{(K_1, K_2, t_{i-1}, t_i)}\big)$. The indicator is $1$ if the price stays inside the range for the whole period. Some range accruals watch several assets.
- A principal-protected note can pair a zero-coupon bond that repays the principal with binaries that pay a fixed bonus.
- An autocallable pays a coupon only if the index is at or above a barrier on the observation date. A cash binary with the same amount, trigger and dates hedges that coupon exactly.

#### *(Vega and Skew)* A binary's vega changes sign near the strike, and a downward skew makes it cost more than its BSM value.

>[!warning] Not Taught in Lecture
>The closed form for a binary's vega and the exact point where it changes sign go beyond the modules. The modules state the sign rule in terms of the forward price and the strike.

A rise in $\sigma$ spreads out the distribution of $S_T$. Suppose the forward price $F = Se^{(r - q)\tau}$ is well above $K$. A wider distribution then moves probability below $K$, and the cash call loses value. Its vega is negative. When $F$ is well below $K$, a wider distribution moves probability above $K$, and the vega is positive. Differentiating $He^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$, with $\partial d_2/\partial\sigma = -d_1/\sigma$, gives the exact vega
$$\mathcal{V}_b = -\frac{He^{-r\tau}\,n(d_2)\,d_1}{\sigma}.$$
Here $n$ is the standard normal density. The sign switches at $d_1 = 0$, where $F = Ke^{-\sigma^2\tau/2}$, slightly below $K$.

The figure plots the vega of a unit cash call with $K = 100$, $r = 4\%$, $q = 1\%$ and $\sigma = 25\%$. The three curves are for three times to expiry, in years. The dots mark the switch points, at $S = 99.39$, $98.48$ and $96.98$. Below them a rise in volatility helps the holder, and above them it hurts.

In the market each strike has its own implied volatility $\sigma(K)$, as in [[2.3.5b Volatility Surface]]. The call price curve is then $c(K) = c_{\text{BSM}}(K, \sigma(K))$, and the chain rule gives
$$b(K) = -\frac{dc}{dK} = e^{-r\tau}N(d_2) - \frac{\partial c}{\partial \sigma}\,\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial K}.$$
The first term is the BSM value at the strike's own volatility. The second is the skew correction, where $\partial c/\partial\sigma$ is the vega of the call with strike $K$. Equity skews slope down, $\partial\sigma/\partial K < 0$, so the skew makes a cash call cost more than its BSM value. A dealer who sells a binary is short this correction. If the skew steepens, the binary gains value and the seller loses. So selling binaries means selling skew. An American binary can pay at any date before $T$. Its price therefore also depends on how volatility varies with maturity. Pricing it needs the whole volatility surface.

#### *(Hedging Near the Trigger)* Near $K$ and close to expiry, a binary's Greeks are large and change fast, so dealers prefer static hedges.

>[!warning] Not Taught in Lecture
>The closed form for the binary's gamma below goes beyond the modules.

The delta of a cash call is
$$\Delta_b = \frac{He^{-r\tau}\,n(d_2)}{S\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}.$$
At $S = K$ it grows like $1/\sqrt{\tau}$ as expiry nears. The gamma, $\Gamma_b = -He^{-r\tau}n(d_2)\,d_1/(S^2\sigma^2\tau)$, changes sign at $d_1 = 0$, as the vega does. Take $H = \$1$ million, $K = 100$, $\sigma = 25\%$, $r = 4\%$ and $q = 1\%$, with $0.01$ years left. A delta hedge holds $159{,}513$ shares at $S = 100$. It holds $20{,}442$ shares at $S = 95$ and $22{,}645$ at $S = 105$. So a $\$5$ move away from the strike forces a trade of about $137{,}000$ to $139{,}000$ shares. A static hedge buys the call spread once and holds it to expiry. The spread's gamma and vega offset the binary's, except within $\eta$ of the strike. The dealer accepts a small, known payoff gap near $K$ in exchange for no rebalancing.

# Derivation

We want the values of the cash and asset binaries and the identity $b(K) = -\partial c/\partial K$.

The [[2.3.3f Black-Scholes-Merton Formula|BSM formula]] splits the call price into an asset part and a cash part,
$$c = e^{-r\tau}\hat{\mathbb{E}}\big[S_TI_K\big] - Ke^{-r\tau}\hat{\mathbb{E}}\big[I_K\big] = Se^{-q\tau}N(d_1) - Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2).$$
Here $\hat{\mathbb{E}}$ is the risk-neutral expectation. The first term is the asset call, and the second is $K$ unit cash calls. So a cash call paying $H$ is worth $He^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$. The puts use $1 - I_K$ in place of $I_K$ and $N(-x) = 1 - N(x)$.

For the strike derivative, both $d_1$ and $d_2$ have $\partial d_i/\partial K = -1/(K\sigma\sqrt{\tau})$. Differentiating $c$ in $K$ gives
$$\frac{\partial c}{\partial K} = -\frac{Se^{-q\tau}n(d_1) - Ke^{-r\tau}n(d_2)}{K\sigma\sqrt{\tau}} - e^{-r\tau}N(d_2).$$
The two densities satisfy $Se^{-q\tau}n(d_1) = Ke^{-r\tau}n(d_2)$, as shown in [[2.3.4b Gamma and Theta]]. So the fraction is zero, and $-\partial c/\partial K = e^{-r\tau}N(d_2) = b(K)$.

# Examples

>[!example] (Easy) Pricing Cash and Asset Binaries
>A stock trades at $\$52$ and pays a continuous dividend yield of $1\%$. Its volatility is $25\%$, and the risk-free rate is $3\%$ per year with continuous compounding. A dealer prices nine-month European binaries with trigger $K = \$50$. The cash call pays $H = \$10$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the values of the cash call and the asset call, build the European call from binaries, and check that the cash call and the cash put together are worth a bond.
>>Here $\tau = 0.75$ and $\sigma\sqrt{\tau} = 0.2165$. The two numbers are
>>$$d_1 = \frac{\ln(52/50) + (0.03 - 0.01 + 0.03125)(0.75)}{0.2165} = \frac{0.03922 + 0.03844}{0.2165} = 0.3587, \qquad d_2 = 0.3587 - 0.2165 = 0.1422.$$
>>A normal table gives $N(d_1) = 0.6401$ and $N(d_2) = 0.5565$. The discount factor is $e^{-0.0225} = 0.9778$. The cash call is worth $10 \times 0.9778 \times 0.5565 = \$5.44$. The asset call is worth $52e^{-0.0075} \times 0.6401 = 51.61 \times 0.6401 = \$33.04$.
>>
>>A European call with strike $\$50$ is one asset call minus $50$ unit cash calls. A unit cash call is worth $\$0.54415$, so the call costs $33.036 - 50 \times 0.54415 = 33.036 - 27.208 = \$5.83$. The BSM formula gives the same $\$5.83$.
>>
>>The cash put pays $\$10$ when $S_T < 50$. With $N(-d_2) = 0.4435$, it is worth $10 \times 0.9778 \times 0.4435 = \$4.34$. The cash call and the cash put together pay $\$10$ in every state. Their total, $5.44 + 4.34 = \$9.78$, equals $10e^{-0.0225}$, the price of a bond paying $\$10$ at $T$.

>[!example] (Medium) Hedging a Sold Binary with a Call Spread
>A client buys a four-month European cash call on a stock from a dealer. It pays $\$100{,}000$ if the stock ends at or above $\$88$. The stock trades at $\$80$ and pays a continuous dividend yield of $1.5\%$. Its implied volatility is $35\%$ at every strike. The risk-free rate is $4.5\%$ per year with continuous compounding.
>
>>[!example]- Find the BSM value of the binary. Find the cost of the dealer's static call-spread hedge with strike gaps of $\$4$ and $\$1$. Then find the sign of the binary's vega and how much of it the hedge offsets.
>>Here $\tau = 1/3$ and $\sigma\sqrt{\tau} = 0.2021$. The two numbers are
>>$$d_1 = \frac{\ln(80/88) + (0.045 - 0.015 + 0.06125)/3}{0.2021} = \frac{-0.09531 + 0.03042}{0.2021} = -0.3211, \qquad d_2 = -0.3211 - 0.2021 = -0.5232.$$
>>So $N(d_2) = 0.30041$, and the discount factor is $e^{-0.015} = 0.98511$. The binary is worth $100{,}000 \times 0.98511 \times 0.30041 = \$29{,}594$.
>>
>>The dealer sold the binary, so it buys the spread that never pays less. With a gap of $\eta = \$4$, it buys $100{,}000/4 = 25{,}000$ calls at $\$84$ and sells $25{,}000$ calls at $\$88$. These calls cost $\$5.07821$ and $\$3.73215$, so the spread costs $25{,}000 \times 1.34606 = \$33{,}652$. With $\eta = \$1$, it buys $100{,}000$ calls at $\$87$ and sells $100{,}000$ at $\$88$. These cost $\$4.03786$ and $\$3.73215$, so the spread costs $100{,}000 \times 0.30571 = \$30{,}571$. The spread with strikes $\$88$ and $\$89$ costs $\$28{,}644$, so the binary's value lies between $\$28{,}644$ and $\$30{,}571$.
>>
>>The hedge pays more than the binary only when $S_T$ ends between $K - \eta$ and $\$88$. In that range the spread pays up to $\$100{,}000$, and the binary pays nothing. The dealer pays for this extra payoff up front. It costs $\$4{,}057$ above the BSM value for $\eta = 4$ and $\$977$ for $\eta = 1$. A quote based on the narrow spread is closer to the BSM value. That hedge needs four times as many calls.
>>
>>The forward price is $80e^{0.03/3} = \$80.80$, well below the trigger of $\$88$. A rise in $\sigma$ moves probability above $\$88$, so the binary's vega is positive. Repricing at $36\%$ raises the binary by $\$304$, and the dealer who sold it loses that amount. The long $\eta = 1$ spread gains $\$281$ over the same move. So the static hedge offsets about $92\%$ of the binary's vega.

>[!example] (Hard) A Range Option Under a Skew
>An index is at $100$ and pays a continuous dividend yield of $1\%$. The risk-free rate is $4\%$ per year with continuous compounding. A client wants a three-month range option that pays $\$10$ if $95 \le S_T < 110$. Implied volatility falls with strike as $\sigma(K) = 22\% - 0.4\% \times (K - 100)$, so $\sigma(95) = 24\%$ and $\sigma(110) = 18\%$.
>
>>[!example]- Price the range option with one volatility of $22\%$, with each strike's own volatility, and with the skew correction. Check the last price with call spreads, and decide whether the seller is long or short skew.
>>The option is long $10$ unit cash calls at $95$ and short $10$ at $110$. Here $\tau = 0.25$, $e^{-r\tau} = 0.9900$ and $Se^{-q\tau}\sqrt{\tau} = 49.875$. The skew slope is $\partial\sigma/\partial K = -0.004$ per dollar of strike.
>>
>>At $K = 95$ with $\sigma = 24\%$, $d_1 = 0.5499$ and $d_2 = 0.4299$, so $e^{-r\tau}N(d_2) = 0.6598$. The call vega is $49.875 \times n(0.5499) = 17.10$. The correction is $17.10 \times 0.004 = 0.0684$, so $b(95) = 0.7282$.
>>
>>At $K = 110$ with $\sigma = 18\%$, $d_1 = -0.9307$ and $d_2 = -1.0207$, so $e^{-r\tau}N(d_2) = 0.1522$. The call vega is $12.90$, the correction is $0.0516$, and $b(110) = 0.2038$.
>>
>>The three prices differ by more than $\$0.40$.
>>- With one volatility of $22\%$ at both strikes, the range option is worth $\$4.83$.
>>- With each strike's own volatility and no correction, it is worth $10(0.6598 - 0.1522) = \$5.08$.
>>- With the skew correction, it is worth $10(0.7282 - 0.2038) = \$5.24$.
>>
>>For the check, replace each binary by a centered spread with strikes $1$ on either side. Buy $5$ calls at $94$ and sell $5$ at $96$. Sell $5$ calls at $109$ and buy $5$ at $111$. At the skewed volatilities these calls cost $8.7693$, $7.3135$, $1.0393$ and $0.6310$. The portfolio costs $5(8.7693 - 7.3135 - 1.0393 + 0.6310) = \$5.24$. It pays $\$10$ between $96$ and $109$ and ramps near each boundary. The call prices already contain the skew, so the spreads reproduce the corrected price.
>>
>>The seller is short the binary at $95$ and long the binary at $110$. Suppose the slope steepens from $-0.004$ to $-0.005$, with the two strike volatilities unchanged. The range option then gains $10 \times (17.10 - 12.90) \times 0.001 = \$0.042$. The seller loses that amount, so the seller is short skew.

# See Also

- [[2.3.2a Vertical Spread]], the call spread whose narrow limit is a cash binary.
- [[2.3.3f Black-Scholes-Merton Formula]], whose two terms are an asset call and $K$ cash calls.
- [[2.3.5b Volatility Surface]], the skew behind the binary's price correction.
- [[2.3.6.2a Barrier Options]], which switch a call or put on or off when the price touches a level.
- [[2.3.6.3b Autocallables]], whose conditional coupons are hedged with cash binaries.
- [[2.3.6.3d Principal-Protected Notes]], which can pair a zero-coupon bond with binaries.
